title: Your Job Is Handing Out Free Money #Shorts
description:
Many employers add money to your 401(k) when you save, and about 1 in 5 participants don't save enough to get the full match. Your boss isn't hiding it; it's in the plan's fine print. In our example, saving 2% instead of 4% leaves $1,200 a year on the table, which could add up to over $100,000 in 30 years under our assumptions. One catch: company match money may only become fully yours after a vesting period.

Sources:
[S1] Fidelity, Q2 2026 Retirement Analysis (81% of 401(k) participants save enough for the full match): https://newsroom.fidelity.com/pressreleases/fidelity--q2-2026-retirement-analysis--record-savings-rates-help-drive-401-k---403-b--and-ira-balanc/s/bca5d71f-ebda-4289-bdd5-a90abde7feba
[S2] Vanguard, How America Saves 2026: https://workplace.vanguard.com/content/dam/inst/iig-transformation/insights/pdf/has/how-america-saves-2026.pdf
[S3] IRS, Retirement Topics: Vesting: https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-vesting
[S4] IRS, Issue Snapshot: Vesting Schedules for Matching Contributions: https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/issue-snapshot-vesting-schedules-for-matching-contributions

Our own calculation:
[D1] $60,000 salary x 4% match (100% match up to 4% of pay) = $2,400 a year.
[D2] Saving only 2% gets $1,200 in match, so $1,200 a year is missed.
[D3] $1,200 a year for 30 years at 7% a year after inflation (end-of-year deposits) = about $113,353 in today's dollars. The 7% return is an assumption for illustration, not guaranteed. No taxes or fees in the math.
